The post Review: East Brother Czech Dark Lager appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s been five years since we’ve checked in with Richmond, California-based East Brother Beer Co., but the release of a new Czech-style dark lager provides the perfect opportunity to reconnect.

A reddish coffee-dark in color, the beer is distinguished from German dark beers by its heavily bready character, pretzel-like with a smear of caramel sauce on top. There’s no torched coffee character, but rather the aroma and flavor of heavily toasted breadcrumbs made from Pumpernickel. At the same time a lively sweetness brightens everything up (albeit giving the finish a little too much molasses character), culminating in a finishing note of bittersweet drinking chocolate.

5.7% abv.

A- / $12 per 4-pack of 16 oz cans

title: Review: Old Elk Whiskey 10 Years Old – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Wheat Whiskey
summary:
Old Elk was founded in Fort Collins, Colorado, in 2013 by Curt and Nancy Richardson, who are best known as the creators of OtterBox. The post Review: Old Elk Whiskey 10 Years Old – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Wheat Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Old Elk was founded in Fort Collins, Colorado, in 2013 by Curt and Nancy Richardson, who are best known as the creators of OtterBox. Rather than wait years for whiskey distilled in-house to reach maturity, the company partnered with Indiana’s MGP, where whiskey was distilled to proprietary recipes developed specifically for Old Elk. Central to that relationship was legendary distiller Greg Metze. After nearly four decades at MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, Metze helped develop several exclusive mashbills for Old Elk while still at MGP before joining the company as Master Distiller in 2016.

In July 2026, Old Elk released three expressions distilled during Metze’s early involvement with the brand: Old Elk Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old, Old Elk Wheated Bourbon 10 Years Old, and Old Elk Wheat Whiskey 10 Years Old.

A defining part of Old Elk’s production philosophy is its proprietary Slow Cut proofing process, which is used for every whiskey bottled below cask strength. Instead of adding all of the proofing water at one time, the distillery introduces small amounts over several weeks.

When water and alcohol are combined, an exothermic reaction occurs, generating heat. At commercial blending volumes, adding a large quantity of water all at once can raise the whiskey’s temperature enough to increase evaporation of some of its most delicate volatile aroma compounds. Although the whiskey is not literally boiled, lighter esters, aldehydes, and other congeners that contribute aroma and flavor can be reduced through rapid proofing.

By reducing proof in small increments, Old Elk limits the amount of heat generated with each addition of water, helping preserve more of the aromatic compounds created during fermentation, distillation, and years  in the barrel. The objective is not to alter the whiskey itself, but to retain as much of its original aroma, flavor, and mouthfeel as possible by reducing the loss of those volatile compounds during proofing.

Whether the results are dramatic or difficult to detect is ultimately for each drinker to determine, but Slow Cut represents a science-based approach that few American distilleries have made such a prominent part of their production process.

After more than ten years in oak, what did Old Elk and its Slow Cut proofing process ultimately deliver?

Old Elk Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old Review

Old Elk Straight Bourbon is a blend of 58 barrels built around an atypical mashbill of 51% corn, 34% malted barley, and 15% rye. The distillate entered the barrel at 115 proof using casks fitted with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves from Speyside, Seguin Moreau, and Independent Stave Company. Barrel ages ranged from 10 years, 6 months, and 15 days to 10 years, 7 months, and 2 days. During more than a decade of maturation, some barrels aged in a rickhouse, while others aged in a palletized warehouse. Although Old Elk is headquartered in Colorado, several barrels spent little time there, while others remained in the state for as long as three years. Before Slow Cut proofing, the blend’s natural harvest proof measured 115.2.

The nose opens with old barn wood that has shed much of its tannic edge before moving into cherry pipe tobacco, with the medicinal side of the cherry standing out more than the sweeter side. Given additional time in the glass, cinnamon graham crackers and citronella begin to appear. More than ten years in oak is certainly apparent, yet the tannins never become unbalanced. Everything points to well-managed maturation throughout the aging process.

The palate heads in a completely different direction. Strawberry hard candy and Watermelon Hubba Bubba gum arrive immediately, offering two clearly defined fruit notes with pronounced sweetness. Both come across as artificial fruit, and I do not mind that at all since the profile brought me back to my youth. Early on, the whiskey is driven almost entirely by those candy-like fruit notes before a touch of clove begins to show across the mid-palate.

The finish continues the sweet profile as vanilla almond milk joins pink cotton candy and ripe peaches. As it continues, the peach gradually turns away from juicy fruit and toward the tannic quality of peach skin.

I found this bourbon highly enjoyable, although its sweetness after more than a decade in the barrel came as a surprise. Rather than drawing significant tannins from the oak, it seems to have taken on more of the wood’s natural sugars. Bourbons this sweet are not usually what I reach for, yet this one is easy to enjoy and should appeal to a wide range of drinkers, including those who are newer to bourbon. 105 proof. A- / $70

Old Elk Wheated Bourbon 10 Years Old Review

This wheated bourbon is a 53-barrel blend distilled from a mashbill of 51% corn, 45% soft red winter wheat, and 4% malted barley, entering the barrel at 120 proof. The casks came from Speyside and Seguin Moreau, built with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves. Every barrel spent 10 years and 7.5 months maturing before batching. Prior to Slow Cut proof reduction, the blend’s natural harvest proof stood at 110.6.

The aroma immediately brings to mind sugar cookie dough, much like opening a tube of Pillsbury sugar cookie dough from the grocery store. Macadamia nuts arrive shortly afterward, followed by dried apricots. Cooked bamboo shoots make an unexpected appearance as well. It is an unusual note, yet it fits comfortably within the profile.

The first sip is heavily influenced by ginger ale, though not in its usual form. Instead, it resembles a fountain pour where the syrup ratio is turned up, giving the drink a denser, sweeter profile. Pralines build on that sugary opening before diluted lemonade enters across the mid-palate. Frosted Shredded Wheat cereal follows, adding another easily identifiable note.

Sweetness remains the dominant theme through the finish as maraschino cherry joins Cool Whip. Near the end, eucalyptus and clove provide some needed distinction.

Even after more than a decade in oak, there is no sign that the barrels pushed the whiskey too far. Likewise, the excessive grassy quality that can sometimes accompany wheated bourbons never develops. I enjoyed this bourbon from start to finish, although dialing back the sweetness just a little would have made for a more complete pour. 105 proof. B+ / $70

Old Elk Straight Wheat Whiskey 10 Years Old Review

While wheated bourbons are widely available, wheat whiskey remains a far less common category. Old Elk’s expression is a 57-barrel blend distilled from a mashbill of 96% wheat and 4% malted barley, entering the barrel at 120 proof. Like the wheated bourbon, it matured in casks from Speyside and Seguin Moreau with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves. Barrel ages ranged from 10 years, 5 months, and 19 days to 11 years, 3 months, and 28 days. Before Slow Cut proofing, the blend’s natural harvest proof measured 112.5.

From the first nosing, this whiskey presents considerably more oak than either of its stablemates. Burnt brown sugar and Red Hots candies arrive first, followed by pecan wood smoke. A vegetal note resembling yellow bell pepper adds an unexpected turn before cream soda residue rounds things out. Compared with the distillery’s straight bourbon and wheated bourbon, this bouquet lines up more closely with what many drinkers would expect from whiskey that has spent more than a decade in the barrel.

The palate opens with dried papaya alongside the tannic bite of red grape skin. Dry hard cider develops across the mid-palate, followed by French toast served without maple syrup.

Oak remains front and center through the finish. Slightly astringent black tea introduces a finish that drinks a touch hotter than expected before giving way to cherry pie with both the filling and crust just past the ideal point of baking. At times, the astringency pushes a little harder than I prefer.

What I found most interesting is how differently more than a decade in oak shaped this wheat whiskey compared to its companions. The wheated bourbon and straight bourbon both favored sweetness and fruit with very little astringency, while this release traveled in the opposite direction, drawing considerably more tannin from the barrel. 103 proof. B / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: 3 Oregon Roses from Stoller Wines, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Elouan, Stoller Family Estate, and Chehalem may not be near one another (Elouan is in California and Chehalem is in Oregon), but all are part of the Stoller Wine Group, based in Oregon’s Willamette Valley.

Today we’re looking at three roses all made from Oregon pinot noir grapes, but representing two different vintages. Thoughts follow.

2024 Elouan Rose Oregon – “Grown in Oregon, made in California.” A pretty, strawberry-forward wine, this 100% pinot noir rose is laced with caramel and touched with floral notes, undercut with layers of lemon and mandarin orange. Juicy but refined, the wine finds a summery footing that meanders its way toward coconut and more tropical notes, concluding on a guava note. A total crowd-pleaser and a great value. A- / $15

2025 Chehalem Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – A considerably drier wine than the Elouan, this 2025 expression hits as rather more traditional, almost rustic at times, with stronger orchard notes of peach and apricot, fading gently into lemon and baked apple as the wine warms up a bit. Again, some coconut gives the finish some exoticism, but it’s much more restrained than the above wine. B+ / $21

2025 Stoller Family Estate Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – Hard-edged at first blush, with a heavily herbal influence that tempers the natural fruit and florals in the mix. I never quite came around to this expression, which remains steadfastly greener than the other expressions in this roundup, and a little weedy at times. That said, a lime sherbet character on the finish perks things up a bit, particularly as the wine warms in glass. Doesn’t really evoke a rose. B / $15

title: Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026
summary:
Since 2021, Japanese distillery Nikka has released regular special editions of single malts from its Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries, offering consumers a way to understand how the styles of the two distilleries compare and contrast. Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release…

The post Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Since 2021, Japanese distillery Nikka has released regular special editions of single malts from its Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries, offering consumers a way to understand how the styles of the two distilleries compare and contrast.

Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release in 2014. For 2026, the whisky finally returns: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old. The label has changed (and the price, of course, has gone up) but the song otherwise remains about the same, “crafted by Nikka Whisky’s current blending team, using carefully reserved whisky batches to ensure consistency and quality for future releases.” The subtext of that: More age statemented whiskies are on the way.

We were excited to get a sample from one of only 1572 bottles available in the U.S. Thoughts follow.

Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 Review

Soft but pretty on the nose, the natural fruit of Miyagikyo comes through right away, It bursts with apple particularly but also finds room for notes of orange blossom and a bit of peach. Fragrant and summery, this isn’t as sweet-smelling as some previous Miyagikyo releases, offering more of a balanced aromatic profile that tempers its fruit with gentle notes of sandalwood and polished oak.

The palate offers similar and quite engaging flavors, apple, pear, and gentle coconut notes all well-represented. The apple notes feel fresh and inviting — red over green — layers of baking spice folded into the sip. The natural woodiness of the whisky is slowly revealed as it develops on the tongue, again sandalwood and silky layers of something darker linger underneath, owing to the influence of new American oak and some sherry staves. Elegant and always inviting throughout the experience, this feels like a much more mature whisky than it is finishing on a cleansing note while evoking a hint of vanilla and nougat.

90 proof.

A / $175 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: NV Sandeman Apitiv Reserve White Port appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In the U.S., white Port continues to grow in popularity — albeit haltingly — with options like Sandeman‘s Apitiv Reserve increasingly available. Made from white grape varietals including (in this case) Malvasia Fina, Códega, Viosinho, Rabigato, Arinto, and Gouveio, white Port is just as sweet as ruby or tawny varieties, but its flavor profile is completely different and much more summery.

Slightly darker in color than the typical white Port, this kicks off with ample sweetness that evokes peaches and pears, both fresh and tinned versions. A floral character adds a light astringency, featuring notes of rose petals and orange flowers. As the wine develops in glass, the fruit notes take on a more caramelized note, weaving into a flambeed banana character, pairing well with lingering tropical overtones. More intense than your typical white Port — just as the color would suggest — it’s a fine option for a refreshing white Port and tonic, or as an aperitif on its own.

A- / $25

title: Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum
summary:
Richard Seale has had an outsized role in the rum resurgence of the last twenty years. His Foursquare distillery helped move the category into the super-premium space after a long exile in beach bars and frat houses. But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail…

The post Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Richard Seale has had an outsized role in the rum resurgence of the last twenty years. His Foursquare distillery helped move the category into the super-premium space after a long exile in beach bars and frat houses. But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail boom, and rebirth of Tiki culture more specifically, gave equal weight to well-made mixing rums.

Launched in 2018, Probitas was designed to meet the cocktailing moment. The blend of Foursquare’s pot- and column-distilled rums from Barbados with pot-distilled rums from Hampden Estate in Jamaica became a go-to white rum cocktail base, adding depth to lighter Caribbean classics. Now the Probitas line is growing with a new addition that looks to fill the darker rum needs of backbars everywhere.

Like the original, Probitas Green Label is a blend of pot- and column-distilled rums. Specifically, it merges unaged twin-column coffey still rum, unaged double-retort pot still rum, and two-year aged double-retort pot still rum from Foursquare Rum Distillery in Barbados with unaged double-retort pot still rum from Hampden Estate. The big distinction appears to be the 10% increase in alcohol content and, perhaps even more significant, the addition of caramel coloring. But this isn’t the sugary, artificial stuff you would find in lower quality rums. How could it be? Richard Seale has been at the vanguard of the additive-free rum movement. As such, he created his own caramel coloring in house by superheating sugar, leaving zero residual sweetness to influence the natural flavors of the blend. Let’s check it out.

Probitas Green Label Blended Rum Review

While classic Probitas is bright and fruity on the nose, this Green Label expression is almost brooding with dark, rich notes of blackstrap molasses, overcooked caramel, and bruleed sugar. As it opens, a little baked pineapple manages to show itself before retreating into more caramelized sugars and an ester-heavy funk that seems even more pronounced than in the classic, despite all those darker sugary notes. With even more time in the glass, things coalesce into dark butterscotch and banana pudding.

The palate is potent, unsurprisingly given the significant uptick in proof, but a smack of brown sugar and cola instantly cools the ethanol and complements undertones of table syrup, clove-studded orange, and candied pineapple. It’s mouthcoating and wonderfully rich, tiptoeing dangerously close to syrupy but never quite getting there. The midpalate is peppery with a pronounced chicory coffee note that adds tannins and grip before eroding into silkier notes of Demerara syrup, five spice, and candied orange peel on a generous, warming finish. Where classic Probitas is ideal for a daiquiri, this new Green Label is a go-to for bolder Tiki drinks or a rum Old Fashioned.

114 proof.

A- / $35

summary:

The post Review: Four Peaks Kilt Lifter appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Four Peaks Brewing, based in Tempe, Arizona, got its start 30 years ago, making it an OG craft brewery. Kilt Lifter was the beer that put Four Peaks on the map, and it remains dominant today: Over the past three decades, Four Peaks has sold more than 800,000 barrels of it, or 200 million pints.

Nevertheless we’ve never covered it. In fact, I’ve never even tasted it until now. So, congrats on 30 years! Here’s a short review.

Ruddy and nutty, Kilt Lifter evokes the tartan on its can design with a bold attack of malt and well-toasted bread, landing somewhere between a savory slice of buttered toast and a breakfast pastry. A gently smokiness leans things toward the former, though the rounded body, a bit gummy at times, always threatens to push the experience back the other way. A finish that touches on vanilla caramel and baked apples makes for a nice counterpoint to some of the warmer elements in the mix. Definitely a winning pick for a cool afternoon.

6% abv.

A- / $12 per six-pack

When it shipped in July 2026, the delay of the spring 2026 edition of Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond was hardly a surprise. These releases invariably hit the market at least a season too late, and Heaven Hill doesn’t seem overly concerned about changing the names of the whiskeys to align with reality. The first release of…

The post Review: Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When it shipped in July 2026, the delay of the spring 2026 edition of Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond was hardly a surprise. These releases invariably hit the market at least a season too late, and Heaven Hill doesn’t seem overly concerned about changing the names of the whiskeys to align with reality.

The first release of 2026 is one of the younger wheated bourbon offerings in the series, all made from stock produced in the spring of 2016. Here we go.

Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition Review

Old Fitzgerald has a reputation for softness, but this expression immediately strikes the nose as even quieter than typical, with the trademark brown banana dominant, layered lightly with cinnamon and nutmeg. A breakfast bowl of oatmeal is not far from the mark, complete with a lightly doughy character that furthers the impression of a morning meal.

The palate is extremely bright and pretty, a chewy dive into nougat and coconut cream, with layers of banana pudding dolloped on top. There’s a ton of vanilla present, all classic elements of the Old Fitz playbook (especially more youthful expressions like this). Hints of orange cream soda add some root beer notes add a more mid-afternoon quality to the experience, but it isn’t until late in the game when some more savory elements finally perk up, with just the lightest hints of barrel char, anise, and torched brassicas. The inherent sweetness of the whiskey fades into a slightly fruity quality on the finish, but only just so, leaving the consumer with an impression of Old Fitz at its absolute gentlest — at least so far.

100 proof.

A- / $150 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

summary:
This is our third round with Daou’s Soul of a Lion, the highest-end offering the Paso Robles winery produces. 2023’s release is 76% cabernet sauvignon, 18% cabernet franc, and 6% petit verdot. As it’s been in the past the wine has an incredible density that suggests drinking it today is less than optimal. Nevertheless, a…

The post Review: 2023 Daou Soul of a Lion Cabernet Sauvignon Adelaida District appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This is our third round with Daou’s Soul of a Lion, the highest-end offering the Paso Robles winery produces. 2023’s release is 76% cabernet sauvignon, 18% cabernet franc, and 6% petit verdot.

As it’s been in the past the wine has an incredible density that suggests drinking it today is less than optimal. Nevertheless, a healthy decanting and some airtime can help this lion to temper its roaring a bit, pushing the 15.2% abv bruiser into gentler territory. After a bit of rest, the wine showcases flavors typical of the expression — raspberry and chocolate in a boozy, Port-like swirl, blackcurrants building as the finish digs its fingernails into you. The finish likens itself to a chocolate-coconut custard, doused in thick raspberry syrup. There’s no anise character to speak of with this expression, so if you’re looking for a more herbal wine this 2023 won’t do the trick. Those in need of a delightful pairing for that ribeye, however, need look no further.

A- / $160 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

title: Review: Diageo Orphan Barrel Project Night Sage Canadian Whisky 25 Years Old
summary:
I’ll hand it to Diageo and its Orphan Barrel Project: “Night Sage” is one of the most non-traditional and creative product names to date. Sure, it sounds more like a Twilight character than a 25 year old Canadian whisky — and even features an owl on the label — but whimsy like that has never stopped…

The post Review: Diageo Orphan Barrel Project Night Sage Canadian Whisky 25 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
I’ll hand it to Diageo and its Orphan Barrel Project: “Night Sage” is one of the most non-traditional and creative product names to date. Sure, it sounds more like a Twilight character than a 25 year old Canadian whisky — and even features an owl on the label — but whimsy like that has never stopped us from taking a product seriously.

Inside the bottle is a blended Canadian whisky with no clear provenance noted aside from being drawn from “the vast Diageo whisky inventory.” Distilled in Ontario and Manitoba, the whisky was matured in two different barrel types: “first-fill oak barrels, used only once prior, and multi-use barrels, both of which previously held other Canadian whisky.”

Let’s taste.

Diageo Orphan Barrel Project Night Sage Canadian Whisky 25 Years Old Review

Racier on the nose than its 45% abv would suggest, this pops with a surprising punch of pepper, both black and white, along with a perhaps telegraphed aroma of dried sage. An oxidized wine along the lines of oloroso sherry quickly makes an appearance, increasing in intensity as it develops in glass.

On the palate, again a boldly winey character quickly arrives, offering some of the doughy and buttery notes that are endemic to Canadian whisky. While a bit vegetal, a significant spice builds the longer you sit with it, resulting in a moderately floral, incense-laden midsection. The longer I sipped on this, the more it evoked perfume.

The finish finds the whisky leaning more into a vermouth character, the florals becoming quite dried and especially perfumy, even a little soapy at times. While it’s a bit much for my taste, that’s all par for the course for what is typically grain-heavy Canadian whisky, of course — and a sign that you are in fact getting what you paid for.

90 proof.

B+ / $225 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
Since Duckhorn acquired the Sonoma-Cutrer winery in 2024, we’ve watched the operation shift and evolve. Today we check in to see how things are progressing with a look at one of its most visible whites: Sonoma-Cutrer Chardonnay Sonoma Coast.

Spoiler: Somebody hit the oak button a few too many times this year, as this 2024 chardonnay is way over the top when it comes to vanilla and coconut cream notes — quite over the top, really. Aggressive on the attack, serving this ice cold helps coax out a little lemon character, especially on the finish, though otherwise the wine can feel decidedly one-note. I thought we were past the days of overt oak bombs, but remaining fans of the style should take note. C / $25

title: Review: Bernheim Original Wheat Whiskey 20th Anniversary Limited Edition
summary:
Has it really been 20 years since Heaven Hill dropped the first wheat whiskey on us? How time flies. While it didn’t exactly set the whiskey world on fire at the time, Bernheim Original was still an early innovation that helped fuel a decades-long boom in American whiskey experimentation and craft. The post Review: Bernheim Original Wheat Whiskey 20th Anniversary Limited Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Has it really been 20 years since Heaven Hill dropped the first wheat whiskey on us? How time flies. While it didn’t exactly set the whiskey world on fire at the time, Bernheim Original was still an early innovation that helped fuel a decades-long boom in American whiskey experimentation and craft. To honor that legacy, Heaven Hill bottled a special anniversary edition Bernheim. And we somehow missed the news when it dropped earlier this year.

Bernheim Original carries a 7-year age statement, and the barrel proof expressions are reportedly aged between seven and nine years. This special release is a bit older, drawn from barrels aged a minimum of 10 years. And while not technically barrel proof, it certainly could be. With its double digit age statement and generous alcohol strength, let’s see how this wheater stacks up.

Bernheim Original Wheat Whiskey 20th Anniversary Limited Edition Review

This is a big whiskey, but not nearly as racy and energetic as the bi-annual barrel proof Bernheims. The nose is surprisingly mellow with warm notes of cinnamon stick, caramel apple, vanilla buttercream, and undertones of chewy fudge. It’s a bit austere initially compared to Heaven Hill’s other wheat whiskeys, but as it opens, the aroma concentrates and deepens, layering on dark brown sugar and black cherry compote.

The palate is every bit the effusive, high octane wheat whiskey we’ve come to expect from the brand, delivering big, well-spiced notes of grated nutmeg, toasted marshmallow, and Mexican chocolate that transition to dark berry jams and cocktail cherry on the midpalate. The heat is nicely integrated, simmering across the sip with a hugging, chili pepper warmth, but it’s not nearly as minty as other high proof Bernheims. The texture is round and oily with a bit more weight than those younger barrel proof expressions, and there’s also more oak in the mix that presents mostly on the back end, adding some welcome grip to an otherwise silky and lengthy conclusion of butterscotch, baking chocolate, and cherry pie. It ranks among the best that Bernheim has delivered to date.

115 proof.

A- / $85 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
It’s been five years since we’ve checked in with Richmond, California-based East Brother Beer Co., but the release of a new Czech-style dark lager provides the perfect opportunity to reconnect.

A reddish coffee-dark in color, the beer is distinguished from German dark beers by its heavily bready character, pretzel-like with a smear of caramel sauce on top. There’s no torched coffee character, but rather the aroma and flavor of heavily toasted breadcrumbs made from Pumpernickel. At the same time a lively sweetness brightens everything up (albeit giving the finish a little too much molasses character), culminating in a finishing note of bittersweet drinking chocolate.

5.7% abv.

A- / $12 per 4-pack of 16 oz cans

title: Review: Old Elk Whiskey 10 Years Old – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Wheat Whiskey
summary:
Old Elk was founded in Fort Collins, Colorado, in 2013 by Curt and Nancy Richardson, who are best known as the creators of OtterBox. Rather than wait years for whiskey distilled in-house to reach maturity, the company partnered with Indiana’s MGP, where whiskey was distilled to proprietary recipes developed specifically for Old Elk. Central to…

The post Review: Old Elk Whiskey 10 Years Old – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Wheat Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Old Elk was founded in Fort Collins, Colorado, in 2013 by Curt and Nancy Richardson, who are best known as the creators of OtterBox. Rather than wait years for whiskey distilled in-house to reach maturity, the company partnered with Indiana’s MGP, where whiskey was distilled to proprietary recipes developed specifically for Old Elk. Central to that relationship was legendary distiller Greg Metze. After nearly four decades at MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, Metze helped develop several exclusive mashbills for Old Elk while still at MGP before joining the company as Master Distiller in 2016.

In July 2026, Old Elk released three expressions distilled during Metze’s early involvement with the brand: Old Elk Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old, Old Elk Wheated Bourbon 10 Years Old, and Old Elk Wheat Whiskey 10 Years Old.

A defining part of Old Elk’s production philosophy is its proprietary Slow Cut proofing process, which is used for every whiskey bottled below cask strength. Instead of adding all of the proofing water at one time, the distillery introduces small amounts over several weeks.

When water and alcohol are combined, an exothermic reaction occurs, generating heat. At commercial blending volumes, adding a large quantity of water all at once can raise the whiskey’s temperature enough to increase evaporation of some of its most delicate volatile aroma compounds. Although the whiskey is not literally boiled, lighter esters, aldehydes, and other congeners that contribute aroma and flavor can be reduced through rapid proofing.

By reducing proof in small increments, Old Elk limits the amount of heat generated with each addition of water, helping preserve more of the aromatic compounds created during fermentation, distillation, and years  in the barrel. The objective is not to alter the whiskey itself, but to retain as much of its original aroma, flavor, and mouthfeel as possible by reducing the loss of those volatile compounds during proofing.

Whether the results are dramatic or difficult to detect is ultimately for each drinker to determine, but Slow Cut represents a science-based approach that few American distilleries have made such a prominent part of their production process.

After more than ten years in oak, what did Old Elk and its Slow Cut proofing process ultimately deliver?

Old Elk Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old Review

Old Elk Straight Bourbon is a blend of 58 barrels built around an atypical mashbill of 51% corn, 34% malted barley, and 15% rye. The distillate entered the barrel at 115 proof using casks fitted with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves from Speyside, Seguin Moreau, and Independent Stave Company. Barrel ages ranged from 10 years, 6 months, and 15 days to 10 years, 7 months, and 2 days. During more than a decade of maturation, some barrels aged in a rickhouse, while others aged in a palletized warehouse. Although Old Elk is headquartered in Colorado, several barrels spent little time there, while others remained in the state for as long as three years. Before Slow Cut proofing, the blend’s natural harvest proof measured 115.2.

The nose opens with old barn wood that has shed much of its tannic edge before moving into cherry pipe tobacco, with the medicinal side of the cherry standing out more than the sweeter side. Given additional time in the glass, cinnamon graham crackers and citronella begin to appear. More than ten years in oak is certainly apparent, yet the tannins never become unbalanced. Everything points to well-managed maturation throughout the aging process.

The palate heads in a completely different direction. Strawberry hard candy and Watermelon Hubba Bubba gum arrive immediately, offering two clearly defined fruit notes with pronounced sweetness. Both come across as artificial fruit, and I do not mind that at all since the profile brought me back to my youth. Early on, the whiskey is driven almost entirely by those candy-like fruit notes before a touch of clove begins to show across the mid-palate.

The finish continues the sweet profile as vanilla almond milk joins pink cotton candy and ripe peaches. As it continues, the peach gradually turns away from juicy fruit and toward the tannic quality of peach skin.

I found this bourbon highly enjoyable, although its sweetness after more than a decade in the barrel came as a surprise. Rather than drawing significant tannins from the oak, it seems to have taken on more of the wood’s natural sugars. Bourbons this sweet are not usually what I reach for, yet this one is easy to enjoy and should appeal to a wide range of drinkers, including those who are newer to bourbon. 105 proof. A- / $70

Old Elk Wheated Bourbon 10 Years Old Review

This wheated bourbon is a 53-barrel blend distilled from a mashbill of 51% corn, 45% soft red winter wheat, and 4% malted barley, entering the barrel at 120 proof. The casks came from Speyside and Seguin Moreau, built with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves. Every barrel spent 10 years and 7.5 months maturing before batching. Prior to Slow Cut proof reduction, the blend’s natural harvest proof stood at 110.6.

The aroma immediately brings to mind sugar cookie dough, much like opening a tube of Pillsbury sugar cookie dough from the grocery store. Macadamia nuts arrive shortly afterward, followed by dried apricots. Cooked bamboo shoots make an unexpected appearance as well. It is an unusual note, yet it fits comfortably within the profile.

The first sip is heavily influenced by ginger ale, though not in its usual form. Instead, it resembles a fountain pour where the syrup ratio is turned up, giving the drink a denser, sweeter profile. Pralines build on that sugary opening before diluted lemonade enters across the mid-palate. Frosted Shredded Wheat cereal follows, adding another easily identifiable note.

Sweetness remains the dominant theme through the finish as maraschino cherry joins Cool Whip. Near the end, eucalyptus and clove provide some needed distinction.

Even after more than a decade in oak, there is no sign that the barrels pushed the whiskey too far. Likewise, the excessive grassy quality that can sometimes accompany wheated bourbons never develops. I enjoyed this bourbon from start to finish, although dialing back the sweetness just a little would have made for a more complete pour. 105 proof. B+ / $70

Old Elk Straight Wheat Whiskey 10 Years Old Review

While wheated bourbons are widely available, wheat whiskey remains a far less common category. Old Elk’s expression is a 57-barrel blend distilled from a mashbill of 96% wheat and 4% malted barley, entering the barrel at 120 proof. Like the wheated bourbon, it matured in casks from Speyside and Seguin Moreau with #2 charred heads and #4 charred staves. Barrel ages ranged from 10 years, 5 months, and 19 days to 11 years, 3 months, and 28 days. Before Slow Cut proofing, the blend’s natural harvest proof measured 112.5.

From the first nosing, this whiskey presents considerably more oak than either of its stablemates. Burnt brown sugar and Red Hots candies arrive first, followed by pecan wood smoke. A vegetal note resembling yellow bell pepper adds an unexpected turn before cream soda residue rounds things out. Compared with the distillery’s straight bourbon and wheated bourbon, this bouquet lines up more closely with what many drinkers would expect from whiskey that has spent more than a decade in the barrel.

The palate opens with dried papaya alongside the tannic bite of red grape skin. Dry hard cider develops across the mid-palate, followed by French toast served without maple syrup.

Oak remains front and center through the finish. Slightly astringent black tea introduces a finish that drinks a touch hotter than expected before giving way to cherry pie with both the filling and crust just past the ideal point of baking. At times, the astringency pushes a little harder than I prefer.

What I found most interesting is how differently more than a decade in oak shaped this wheat whiskey compared to its companions. The wheated bourbon and straight bourbon both favored sweetness and fruit with very little astringency, while this release traveled in the opposite direction, drawing considerably more tannin from the barrel. 103 proof. B / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: 3 Oregon Roses from Stoller Wines, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Elouan, Stoller Family Estate, and Chehalem may not be near one another (Elouan is in California and Chehalem is in Oregon), but all are part of the Stoller Wine Group, based in Oregon’s Willamette Valley.

Today we’re looking at three roses all made from Oregon pinot noir grapes, but representing two different vintages. Thoughts follow.

2024 Elouan Rose Oregon – “Grown in Oregon, made in California.” A pretty, strawberry-forward wine, this 100% pinot noir rose is laced with caramel and touched with floral notes, undercut with layers of lemon and mandarin orange. Juicy but refined, the wine finds a summery footing that meanders its way toward coconut and more tropical notes, concluding on a guava note. A total crowd-pleaser and a great value. A- / $15

2025 Chehalem Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – A considerably drier wine than the Elouan, this 2025 expression hits as rather more traditional, almost rustic at times, with stronger orchard notes of peach and apricot, fading gently into lemon and baked apple as the wine warms up a bit. Again, some coconut gives the finish some exoticism, but it’s much more restrained than the above wine. B+ / $21

2025 Stoller Family Estate Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – Hard-edged at first blush, with a heavily herbal influence that tempers the natural fruit and florals in the mix. I never quite came around to this expression, which remains steadfastly greener than the other expressions in this roundup, and a little weedy at times. That said, a lime sherbet character on the finish perks things up a bit, particularly as the wine warms in glass. Doesn’t really evoke a rose. B / $15

title: Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026
summary:

Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release…

The post Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Since 2021, Japanese distillery Nikka has released regular special editions of single malts from its Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries, offering consumers a way to understand how the styles of the two distilleries compare and contrast.

Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release in 2014. For 2026, the whisky finally returns: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old. The label has changed (and the price, of course, has gone up) but the song otherwise remains about the same, “crafted by Nikka Whisky’s current blending team, using carefully reserved whisky batches to ensure consistency and quality for future releases.” The subtext of that: More age statemented whiskies are on the way.

We were excited to get a sample from one of only 1572 bottles available in the U.S. Thoughts follow.

Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 Review

Soft but pretty on the nose, the natural fruit of Miyagikyo comes through right away, It bursts with apple particularly but also finds room for notes of orange blossom and a bit of peach. Fragrant and summery, this isn’t as sweet-smelling as some previous Miyagikyo releases, offering more of a balanced aromatic profile that tempers its fruit with gentle notes of sandalwood and polished oak.

The palate offers similar and quite engaging flavors, apple, pear, and gentle coconut notes all well-represented. The apple notes feel fresh and inviting — red over green — layers of baking spice folded into the sip. The natural woodiness of the whisky is slowly revealed as it develops on the tongue, again sandalwood and silky layers of something darker linger underneath, owing to the influence of new American oak and some sherry staves. Elegant and always inviting throughout the experience, this feels like a much more mature whisky than it is finishing on a cleansing note while evoking a hint of vanilla and nougat.

90 proof.

A / $175 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: NV Sandeman Apitiv Reserve White Port appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In the U.S., white Port continues to grow in popularity — albeit haltingly — with options like Sandeman‘s Apitiv Reserve increasingly available. Made from white grape varietals including (in this case) Malvasia Fina, Códega, Viosinho, Rabigato, Arinto, and Gouveio, white Port is just as sweet as ruby or tawny varieties, but its flavor profile is completely different and much more summery.

Slightly darker in color than the typical white Port, this kicks off with ample sweetness that evokes peaches and pears, both fresh and tinned versions. A floral character adds a light astringency, featuring notes of rose petals and orange flowers. As the wine develops in glass, the fruit notes take on a more caramelized note, weaving into a flambeed banana character, pairing well with lingering tropical overtones. More intense than your typical white Port — just as the color would suggest — it’s a fine option for a refreshing white Port and tonic, or as an aperitif on its own.

A- / $25

title: Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum
summary:
Richard Seale has had an outsized role in the rum resurgence of the last twenty years. His Foursquare distillery helped move the category into the super-premium space after a long exile in beach bars and frat houses. But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail…

The post Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Richard Seale has had an outsized role in the rum resurgence of the last twenty years. His Foursquare distillery helped move the category into the super-premium space after a long exile in beach bars and frat houses. But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail boom, and rebirth of Tiki culture more specifically, gave equal weight to well-made mixing rums.

Launched in 2018, Probitas was designed to meet the cocktailing moment. The blend of Foursquare’s pot- and column-distilled rums from Barbados with pot-distilled rums from Hampden Estate in Jamaica became a go-to white rum cocktail base, adding depth to lighter Caribbean classics. Now the Probitas line is growing with a new addition that looks to fill the darker rum needs of backbars everywhere.

Like the original, Probitas Green Label is a blend of pot- and column-distilled rums. Specifically, it merges unaged twin-column coffey still rum, unaged double-retort pot still rum, and two-year aged double-retort pot still rum from Foursquare Rum Distillery in Barbados with unaged double-retort pot still rum from Hampden Estate. The big distinction appears to be the 10% increase in alcohol content and, perhaps even more significant, the addition of caramel coloring. But this isn’t the sugary, artificial stuff you would find in lower quality rums. How could it be? Richard Seale has been at the vanguard of the additive-free rum movement. As such, he created his own caramel coloring in house by superheating sugar, leaving zero residual sweetness to influence the natural flavors of the blend. Let’s check it out.

Probitas Green Label Blended Rum Review

While classic Probitas is bright and fruity on the nose, this Green Label expression is almost brooding with dark, rich notes of blackstrap molasses, overcooked caramel, and bruleed sugar. As it opens, a little baked pineapple manages to show itself before retreating into more caramelized sugars and an ester-heavy funk that seems even more pronounced than in the classic, despite all those darker sugary notes. With even more time in the glass, things coalesce into dark butterscotch and banana pudding.

The palate is potent, unsurprisingly given the significant uptick in proof, but a smack of brown sugar and cola instantly cools the ethanol and complements undertones of table syrup, clove-studded orange, and candied pineapple. It’s mouthcoating and wonderfully rich, tiptoeing dangerously close to syrupy but never quite getting there. The midpalate is peppery with a pronounced chicory coffee note that adds tannins and grip before eroding into silkier notes of Demerara syrup, five spice, and candied orange peel on a generous, warming finish. Where classic Probitas is ideal for a daiquiri, this new Green Label is a go-to for bolder Tiki drinks or a rum Old Fashioned.

114 proof.

A- / $35

The post Review: Four Peaks Kilt Lifter appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Four Peaks Brewing, based in Tempe, Arizona, got its start 30 years ago, making it an OG craft brewery. Kilt Lifter was the beer that put Four Peaks on the map, and it remains dominant today: Over the past three decades, Four Peaks has sold more than 800,000 barrels of it, or 200 million pints.

Nevertheless we’ve never covered it. In fact, I’ve never even tasted it until now. So, congrats on 30 years! Here’s a short review.

Ruddy and nutty, Kilt Lifter evokes the tartan on its can design with a bold attack of malt and well-toasted bread, landing somewhere between a savory slice of buttered toast and a breakfast pastry. A gently smokiness leans things toward the former, though the rounded body, a bit gummy at times, always threatens to push the experience back the other way. A finish that touches on vanilla caramel and baked apples makes for a nice counterpoint to some of the warmer elements in the mix. Definitely a winning pick for a cool afternoon.

6% abv.

A- / $12 per six-pack

The first release of…

The post Review: Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When it shipped in July 2026, the delay of the spring 2026 edition of Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond was hardly a surprise. These releases invariably hit the market at least a season too late, and Heaven Hill doesn’t seem overly concerned about changing the names of the whiskeys to align with reality.

The first release of 2026 is one of the younger wheated bourbon offerings in the series, all made from stock produced in the spring of 2016. Here we go.

Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition Review

Old Fitzgerald has a reputation for softness, but this expression immediately strikes the nose as even quieter than typical, with the trademark brown banana dominant, layered lightly with cinnamon and nutmeg. A breakfast bowl of oatmeal is not far from the mark, complete with a lightly doughy character that furthers the impression of a morning meal.

The palate is extremely bright and pretty, a chewy dive into nougat and coconut cream, with layers of banana pudding dolloped on top. There’s a ton of vanilla present, all classic elements of the Old Fitz playbook (especially more youthful expressions like this). Hints of orange cream soda add some root beer notes add a more mid-afternoon quality to the experience, but it isn’t until late in the game when some more savory elements finally perk up, with just the lightest hints of barrel char, anise, and torched brassicas. The inherent sweetness of the whiskey fades into a slightly fruity quality on the finish, but only just so, leaving the consumer with an impression of Old Fitz at its absolute gentlest — at least so far.

100 proof.

A- / $150 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
